# Why write code at all? {.section-break}

## The alternative is worse {.smaller}

You *could* do all of this by pointing and clicking in Excel or SPSS.
Here is why we don't:

::: incremental
- **You can check your own work.** Six months from now, "how did I
  define preterm?" has an answer.
- **Your supervisor can check your work.** So can a peer reviewer, and
  so can you when a reviewer asks.
- **The Methods section writes itself.** Your script *is* the methods
  section.
- **Data changes. Constantly.** New cases arrive, a variable gets
  corrected, you discover an exclusion you missed. Re-running a script
  takes 30 seconds. Redoing 40 clicks takes an afternoon and introduces
  new errors.
- **Reproducibility is now an expectation**, from CIHR, from journals,
  and from ICES.
:::

. . .

::: keypoint
A script is a permanent, auditable record of every decision you made
about the data. That record is the actual scientific product — the
p-value is just the last line.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The landscape {.smaller}

|   | **R** | **SAS** | **Python** | **Stata** |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| Cost | Free | \$\$\$ (free for students) | Free | \$\$ |
| Strength | Stats, graphics, new methods | Very large data, validated pipelines | ML / deep learning, engineering | Econometrics, survey data |
| Epi community | Growing fast | Entrenched | Growing | Strong in health econ |
| New methods appear | First | 5+ years later | First (ML) | Varies |

::: small
**What you will actually meet in Ontario health research:** ICES
analytic environment → **SAS and R**. The Ottawa Hospital Data Warehouse
→ **SAS and R**. BORN Ontario → **SAS and R**. Statistics Canada RDCs →
**SAS, R, Stata**. CHEO/OHRI imaging & ML work → **Python and R**.
:::

. . .

::: keypoint
You do not have to choose. You have to be **literate in SAS** and
**fluent in R**. That is exactly the split of these two sessions.
:::

# R's building blocks {.section-break}

## R is a calculator that remembers things {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 5
2 + 2

7 / 2          # ordinary division
7 %/% 2        # integer division
7 %% 2         # remainder — very handy for age/date arithmetic

sqrt(144)
round(3.14159, 2)
```

::: {.small .muted}
Anything after `#` is a comment. Comment generously — the person reading
your code in six months is you, and you will have forgotten everything.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Assignment: making things stick {.smaller}

Use `<-` to give a value a name. (`=` also works, but `<-` is the
convention and reads as "gets".)

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 6
ga_weeks <- 38.4
birth_weight <- 3250

# names appear in your Environment and can be reused
bw_kg <- birth_weight / 1000
bw_kg

# R is case sensitive and picky about spelling
GA_weeks <- 41
c(ga_weeks, GA_weeks)
```

::: {.callout-tip .smaller appearance="simple"}
**Naming:** lowercase, words separated by `_`, no spaces, don't start
with a number. `birth_weight_g` is a good name. `bw2FINAL` is a crime
against your future self.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Vectors: R's atom {.smaller}

Almost everything in R is a **vector** — an ordered collection of values
*of the same type*. `c()` combines things into one.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 7
ga <- c(38.4, 41.1, 34.0, 39.7, 27.3)

length(ga)
mean(ga)
ga * 7                 # every element, at once — no loop needed
ga < 37                # a logical vector: one TRUE/FALSE per element
sum(ga < 37)           # TRUE counts as 1 → "how many preterm?"
```

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**Vectorisation** is the single biggest mental shift from SAS. In SAS
you think one row at a time. In R you operate on whole columns at once.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The four types you will meet {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
num  <- c(3250, 2410, 4100)          # numeric  (double)
int  <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)                 # integer
chr  <- c("Ottawa", "Kingston")       # character
lgl  <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)          # logical

class(num); class(chr); class(lgl)

# Coercion: mix types and R quietly demotes everything to the "safest" one
mixed <- c(1, 2, "three")
class(mixed)
mixed
```

::: {.callout-warning .smaller appearance="simple"}
That silent coercion is a classic bug source. One stray `"N/A"` typed
into a birth-weight column turns the whole column into text, and
`mean()` then fails.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Your turn: vectors {.smaller}

Five infants' birth weights in grams. Fill in the blanks to get the
**mean in kilograms** and the **number of low-birth-weight (\<2500 g)
infants**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vec
#| min-lines: 6
bw <- c(3250, 2410, 4100, 1980, 3600)

# mean in kilograms
mean(______) / ______

# how many below 2500 g?
sum(bw ______ 2500)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_vec"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

`mean()` takes the vector itself. To convert grams to kilograms, divide
by 1000. For the count, you want the comparison operator "less than".
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_vec"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vec
#| solution: true
bw <- c(3250, 2410, 4100, 1980, 3600)

mean(bw) / 1000

sum(bw < 2500)
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Missing values are their own thing {.smaller}

`NA` is not zero, not `""`, and not "unknown text". It is R's explicit
marker for *missing*.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
bw <- c(3250, NA, 4100, 1980, NA)

mean(bw)                  # NA — and that is R protecting you
mean(bw, na.rm = TRUE)    # what you probably wanted

is.na(bw)                 # which ones?
sum(is.na(bw))            # how many?
bw == NA                  # NEVER do this — NA is not comparable
```

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
`mean(x)` returning `NA` is a **feature**. It forces you to notice
missingness and make a deliberate decision, instead of silently
analysing a complete-case subset you never chose.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Factors: categorical variables with rules {.smaller}

A factor is a categorical variable with a fixed set of **levels** and —
critically for us — a **reference level**.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
smoke <- factor(c("no", "yes", "no", "no", "yes"))
smoke
levels(smoke)                 # first level = reference category in every model
table(smoke)

# ordered categories: set the order yourself, don't let R alphabetise
ga_cat <- factor(c("term", "preterm", "term", "very preterm"),
                 levels = c("term", "preterm", "very preterm"))
table(ga_cat)
```

::: {.callout-important .smaller appearance="simple"}
**This matters for your regressions.** The first level is the reference
group. By default R sorts alphabetically, so `"exposed"` beats
`"unexposed"` and your odds ratio comes out upside down. Set levels
explicitly. Always.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Functions, and how to read their help {.smaller}

::::: cols-60-40
::: {}
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 6
x <- c(3250, NA, 4100, 1980)

# arguments can go by position…
round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

# …but naming them is clearer and safer
seq(from = 24, to = 42, by = 2)

quantile(x, probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {}
### Getting help

``` r
?mean            # the help page
args(quantile)   # just the arguments
example(seq)     # runnable examples
```

<p class="small">

Help pages are terse but complete. Read the <b>Arguments</b> and
<b>Examples</b> sections first; skip <b>Details</b> until you need it.

</p>
:::
:::::

# Rectangular data {.section-break}

## Data frames {.smaller}

A **data frame** is what you actually analyse: columns of equal length,
each with its own type. One row = one observation. This is a SAS
dataset, a Stata `.dta`, an Excel sheet.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 9
clinic <- data.frame(
  id        = 1:5,
  site      = c("Ottawa", "Ottawa", "Kingston", "Sudbury", "Kingston"),
  ga_weeks  = c(38.4, 41.1, 34.0, 39.7, 27.3),
  bw_g      = c(3250, 4100, 2280, 3510, 980)
)

clinic
dim(clinic)       # rows, columns
names(clinic)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Looking at a data frame {.smaller}

The first thing you do with *any* dataset, every single time:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
clinic <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5, site = c("Ottawa","Ottawa","Kingston","Sudbury","Kingston"),
  ga_weeks = c(38.4, 41.1, 34.0, 39.7, 27.3), bw_g = c(3250, 4100, 2280, 3510, 980))

str(clinic)          # structure: types and first values
summary(clinic)      # per-column summaries + NA counts
head(clinic, 3)      # first rows
clinic$bw_g          # pull out one column with $
```

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
`str()` and `summary()` before anything else. Every time. They catch the
"birth weight imported as text" and "43% missing" problems before you
waste a week.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Your turn: explore and create {.smaller}

Add a `bw_kg` column and a logical `lbw` flag for birth weight under
2500 g.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_df
#| min-lines: 8
clinic <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5, site = c("Ottawa","Ottawa","Kingston","Sudbury","Kingston"),
  ga_weeks = c(38.4, 41.1, 34.0, 39.7, 27.3), bw_g = c(3250, 4100, 2280, 3510, 980))

# create a new column
clinic$bw_kg <- ______

# a TRUE/FALSE flag for low birth weight
clinic$lbw <- clinic$bw_g ______

clinic
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_df"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

`clinic$bw_g / 1000` gives kilograms. For the flag you need a comparison
that returns `TRUE` when the weight is below 2500.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_df"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_df
#| solution: true
clinic <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5, site = c("Ottawa","Ottawa","Kingston","Sudbury","Kingston"),
  ga_weeks = c(38.4, 41.1, 34.0, 39.7, 27.3), bw_g = c(3250, 4100, 2280, 3510, 980))

clinic$bw_kg <- clinic$bw_g / 1000
clinic$lbw   <- clinic$bw_g < 2500
clinic
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reading real data {.smaller}

Our seminar data is a **synthetic** perinatal dataset: births, maternal
characteristics, and newborn-screening analytes. Structured like the
real thing, entirely made up.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 6
births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")

dim(births)
str(births)
head(births, 4)
```

::: {.small .muted}
`read.csv()` is base R. In the second session we use `readr::read_csv()`, which is
faster, never silently converts text to factors, and tells you what type
it guessed for each column.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## First look — the things that bite {.smaller}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| min-lines: 8
births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")

table(births$sex)                    # look carefully…
summary(births$ga_weeks)
summary(births$birth_weight_g)
sum(is.na(births$ga_weeks))
```

. . .

::: {.callout-warning .smaller appearance="simple"}
**`sex` has four levels: `F`, `M`, `f`, `m`.** A real data-entry
artefact, and the reason your "male" subgroup is missing a third of its
cases. We fix this properly in the second session.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Your turn: interrogate the data {.smaller}

How many births were **preterm** (`ga_weeks < 37`), and what proportion
is that?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_read
#| min-lines: 7
births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")

# how many preterm births?
sum(______)

# what proportion? (mean of a TRUE/FALSE vector = the proportion of TRUEs)
______(births$ga_weeks < 37)

# bonus: mean birth weight among preterm infants only
mean(births$birth_weight_g[______])
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_read"}
<h4>Hint</h4>

`births$ga_weeks < 37` gives you a logical vector. `sum()` counts the
`TRUE`s; `mean()` of the same vector gives the proportion. Square
brackets `[ ]` subset a vector using a logical condition.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_read"}
<h4>Solution</h4>

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_read
#| solution: true
births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")

sum(births$ga_weeks < 37)

mean(births$ga_weeks < 37)

mean(births$birth_weight_g[births$ga_weeks < 37])
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#| autorun: true

births <- read.csv("data/births.csv")

hist(births$ga_weeks, breaks = 30, col = "#8b1d41", border = "white",

# Packages and the working environment {.section-break}

## Packages {.smaller}

Base R is deliberately small. Everything else lives in **packages** —
over 22,000 of them on CRAN.

::::: cols
::: {}
``` r
# ONCE per computer
install.packages("tidyverse")

# EVERY session, in your script
library(tidyverse)
```

<p class="small">

<b>Install once, library every time.</b> Never put
<code>install.packages()</code> in a script you share — it re-downloads
on someone else's machine without asking.

</p>
:::

::: {}
### Worth knowing about

- **tidyverse** — `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `readr`, … (second session)
- **haven** — read SAS `.sas7bdat` files directly
- **janitor** — clean messy variable names
- **gtsummary** / **tableone** — publication "Table 1"
- **survival**, **lme4**, **mice**, **survey**
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {.small .muted}
`pkg::function()` calls a function without loading the whole package —
e.g. `haven::read_sas()`. Useful, and it documents where a function came
from.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## RStudio: the four panes {.smaller}

::::::: ide
::: {}
<b>1 · Source (top-left)</b> Your script. This is the real work. Write
here, not in the console. [Ctrl/Cmd + Enter runs the current
line.]{.muted}
:::

::: {}
<b>2 · Environment (top-right)</b> Every object you've created, with its
size and type. Also the History tab.
:::

::: {}
<b>3 · Console (bottom-left)</b> Where code actually executes. Fine for
throwaway checks — anything you'd want again belongs in the script.
:::

::: {}
<b>4 · Files / Plots / Packages / Help (bottom-right)</b> Your working
directory, your figures, and the help pages.
:::
:::::::

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**The one habit that matters:** work in the Source pane, not the
Console. If it only ever happened in the Console, it didn't happen.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Projects, and never using `setwd()` {.smaller}

::::: cols
::: {}
### Do this

``` r
# File > New Project > New Directory
# then open the .Rproj file

# paths are relative to the project root
births <- read_csv("data/births.csv")
```

<p class="small">

The project root <i>is</i> your working directory. Move the folder,
email it, put it on OneDrive — it still works.

</p>
:::

::: {}
### Not this

``` r
setwd("C:/Users/shawken/Desktop/
       thesis/final/FINAL2/data")
```

<p class="small">

This runs on exactly one computer, until you reorganise your Desktop. It
is the single most common reason a supervisor cannot run a student's
code.

</p>
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip .smaller appearance="simple"}
**Tools \> Global Options \> General:** set *Save workspace to .RData on
exit* to **Never**, and untick *Restore .RData at startup*. You want
your script to rebuild everything from scratch, every time. That is what
reproducible means.
:::

# A working tour of SAS {.section-break background-color="#8b1d41"}

## Why you still need SAS [15 min]{.time} {.smaller}

::: incremental
- **ICES, ICES-uOttawa, TOHDW, CIHI, BORN, StatCan RDCs** all run on it.
  Large linked administrative holdings, decades of validated code, and
  analysts who know it cold.
- It handles data **larger than memory** without you thinking about it —
  R will fall over on a 40-million-row OHIP claims extract where SAS
  shrugs.
- Your supervisor's existing analysis code is probably SAS. You will
  need to read it, and you will need to check it.
- It is **extremely stable**. Code written in 2004 still runs. That is a
  real virtue for a cohort study that has been running since 2004.
:::

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**Goal for the next 15 minutes:** not fluency. Enough SAS literacy to
read someone else's program, run it, and know when the log is lying to
you.
:::

## The whole language, in one idea {.smaller}

SAS has exactly two kinds of step, and everything is one or the other.

::::: cols
::: {}
### `DATA` step

Reads and writes datasets **one row at a time**. Creating variables,
filtering, merging, recoding.

``` sas
DATA preterm;
  SET births;
  IF ga_weeks < 37;
  bw_kg = birth_weight_g / 1000;
RUN;
```
:::

::: {}
### `PROC` step

Does something to a **whole table**. Summarising, tabulating, modelling,
plotting.

``` sas
PROC MEANS DATA=births;
  CLASS site;
  VAR birth_weight_g;
RUN;
```
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**Every statement ends with a semicolon.** A missing `;` is responsible
for roughly 90% of the time you will lose to SAS. Not an exaggeration.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Libraries: where datasets live {.smaller}

``` sas
/* WORK is temporary — everything in it vanishes when SAS closes */
DATA births;          /* really WORK.births */
  SET mylib.births;
RUN;

/* LIBNAME points a nickname at a folder, for permanent storage */
LIBNAME mylib "/home/steven.hawken0/seminar/data";

DATA mylib.births_clean;   /* saved to disk as births_clean.sas7bdat */
  SET births;
RUN;
```

::::: rs
::: r-side
<h4>R equivalent</h4>

``` r
births        # lives in memory only
saveRDS(births, "data/births.rds")
```
:::

::: sas-side
<h4>The mental model</h4>

`WORK.` = R's environment. `LIBNAME` = a folder on disk. Two-level name
= `library.dataset`.
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Demo 1 — make a dataset and look at it {.smaller}

``` sas
DATA clinic;
  INPUT id site $ ga_weeks bw_g;
  bw_kg = bw_g / 1000;
  preterm = (ga_weeks < 37);      /* a 0/1 flag: the condition IS the value */
  DATALINES;
1 Ottawa   38.4 3250
2 Ottawa   41.1 4100
3 Kingston 34.0 2280
4 Sudbury  39.7 3510
5 Kingston 27.3  980
;
RUN;

PROC PRINT DATA=clinic; RUN;
PROC CONTENTS DATA=clinic VARNUM; RUN;
```

::: {.small .muted}
`$` after a variable name means "this one is character". `VARNUM` lists
variables in creation order instead of alphabetically — always use it.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Demo 2 — import, describe, tabulate {.smaller}

``` sas
PROC IMPORT DATAFILE="/home/steven.hawken0/seminar/data/births.csv"
  OUT=births DBMS=CSV REPLACE;
  GETNAMES=YES;
RUN;

PROC FREQ DATA=births;
  TABLES sex site sex*site / NOPERCENT NOCOL;
RUN;

PROC MEANS DATA=births N MEAN STD MIN MAX;
  CLASS site;
  VAR ga_weeks birth_weight_g;
RUN;

PROC UNIVARIATE DATA=births;
  VAR birth_weight_g;
  HISTOGRAM / NORMAL;
RUN;
```

::: {.small .muted}
Use the **Tasks and Utilities → Import Data** wizard once, then copy the
generated code into your program. Next time you run the whole thing from
the script.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Demo 3 — a picture {.smaller}

``` sas
PROC SGPLOT DATA=births;
  HISTOGRAM ga_weeks / BINWIDTH=0.5;
  REFLINE 37 / AXIS=X LINEATTRS=(PATTERN=dash THICKNESS=2);
  TITLE "Gestational age at birth";
RUN;

PROC SGPLOT DATA=births;
  VBOX birth_weight_g / CATEGORY=site;
  TITLE "Birth weight by site";
RUN;

PROC SGPLOT DATA=births;
  SCATTER X=ga_weeks Y=birth_weight_g / GROUP=sex;
  REG X=ga_weeks Y=birth_weight_g;
RUN;
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **Read the log.** Every time. {.smaller}

SAS will happily produce beautiful, confident, *wrong* output and tell
you about it only in the log.

::::: cols
::: {}
### Three words to search for

- [**ERROR**]{style="color:#b00"} — it stopped. You'll notice.
- [**WARNING**]{style="color:#a86a00"} — it kept going. You might not
  notice.
- [**NOTE**]{style="color:#12707a"} — the dangerous one.
:::

::: {}
### The NOTEs that ruin analyses

``` text
NOTE: Invalid numeric data, 'N/A'
NOTE: Missing values were generated
NOTE: MERGE statement has more than
      one dataset with repeats of BY
```
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {.keypoint .smaller}
**Check `N` after every step.** If `births` had 1,239 observations and
your merged dataset has 1,372, you have a problem — and SAS told you
about it in a NOTE you scrolled past. We will do exactly this bug live
in R in the second session.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## R ↔ SAS Rosetta stone {.smaller}

| Task | R (tidyverse) | SAS |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Create dataset | `tibble()` / `data.frame()` | `DATA`; `INPUT`; `DATALINES` |
| Import CSV | `read_csv("f.csv")` | `PROC IMPORT ... DBMS=CSV` |
| Inspect | `str()`, `glimpse()` | `PROC CONTENTS VARNUM` |
| New variable | `mutate(bmi = wt/ht^2)` | `bmi = wt/ht**2;` in a DATA step |
| Keep rows | `filter(ga < 37)` | `IF ga < 37;` or `WHERE` |
| Keep columns | `select(id, ga)` | `KEEP id ga;` |
| Sort | `arrange(desc(bw))` | `PROC SORT; BY DESCENDING bw;` |
| Frequencies | `count(site)` / `table()` | `PROC FREQ; TABLES site;` |
| Group summary | `group_by() |> summarise()` | `PROC MEANS; CLASS ...; VAR ...;` |
| Join | `left_join(a, b, by = "id")` | `MERGE a b; BY id;` or `PROC SQL` |
| Plot | `ggplot()` | `PROC SGPLOT` |
| Linear model | `lm(y ~ x)` | `PROC REG` / `PROC GLM` |
| Logistic model | `glm(y ~ x, family = binomial)` | `PROC LOGISTIC` |
| Survival | `coxph(Surv(t, d) ~ x)` | `PROC PHREG` |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Two SAS habits worth stealing {.smaller}

::::: cols
::: {}
### Comment out, don't delete

``` sas
DATA cohort;
  SET births;
  IF ga_weeks >= 22;
* IF ga_weeks >= 20;   /* prior defn */
RUN;
/* N = 1239 */
```

<p class="small">

Record what each version gave you. Reviewers ask.

</p>
:::

::: {}
### Recovering from unbalanced quotes

``` sas
*'; *"; */;
```

<p class="small">

If a stray quote makes SAS unresponsive, run that line (sometimes
twice). Harmless if nothing is wrong; saves you a restart if something
is. Tape it to your monitor.

</p>
:::
